title: Course Introduction: The Systems Approach & Modeling
summary: Foundational overview of the systems approach, modeling process, model development, and optimization principles.
content:
The Systems Approach

The most effective analytical framework for the solution of problems of meaningful scale or the development of new systems is called the systems approach. There are six essential elements in the procedure:

  • Identify Goals (Problems): The first step in developing a system or in solving a problem is to identify the goals of the system or to specify the problem to be solved, ensuring real goals and real problems (not merely visible symptoms) are specified.
  • Define Objectives: Translate the general goals or problems into specific objectives, defining each objective in precise terms that can be accomplished at a level below the total system level.
  • Generate Alternatives: Produce possible solutions for each objective without permitting preconceived solutions to stifle new approaches, ensuring all feasible alternatives that do not violate internal or external constraints are considered.
  • Evaluate Alternatives and Select Solution(s): Screen and evaluate proposed alternatives based on defined goals and objectives, utilizing management science models to measure effectiveness and select optimal courses of action.
  • Integrate the Solutions: Combine subproblem solutions into a unified solution to the overall problem, assuring compatibility and looking for serendipitous interactions leading to system synergy.
  • Implement the Solution and Monitor Results: Implement identified solutions with careful attention to behavioral details and 'people problems', and monitor results over time to determine effectiveness.

The Use of Feedback: Continuous checking at each stage ensures that alternatives, evaluation criteria, and selected solutions remain in keeping with originally specified goals and objectives.

The Role of Models

Management science is almost exclusively concerned with the development, design, solution, and interpretation of mathematical models. The modeling process consists of five basic elements: abstraction, validation, prediction, evaluation, and revision. Real-world unstructured problems are abstracted into simplified mathematical structures, validated against known situations, used to predict outcomes, and evaluated against actual outcomes over time.

Model Development & Optimization

Optimization is the selection of alternatives that constitute the best known courses of action under some set of objective criteria, subject to constraints defining a region of feasibility. Decision-makers must guard against suboptimization (optimizing at a level below the total system level) and overoptimization, preferring robust 'saucer-type' solutions and satisficing strategies when appropriate.
